title: Contrary to Privately Expressed Negative Views: the Research Settlement, Ten Firms and $1.4 Billion

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the banking fee that the research was there to win. The regulators’ description of Grubman is the mechanism stated as a job title: "the lead research analyst for SSB's telecommunications (telecom) sector and the linchpin for SSB's investment banking efforts in the telecom sector."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the separation between the two, at every firm examined. The enforcement actions "allege that, from approximately mid-1999 through mid-2001 or later, all of the firms engaged in acts and practices that created or maintained inappropriate influence by investment banking over research analysts, thereby imposing conflicts of interest on research analysts that the firms failed to manage in an adequate or appropriate manner. In addition, the regulators found supervisory deficiencies at every firm."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was the published rating, and the charges describe the gap precisely. Blodget "issued fraudulent research under Merrill Lynch's name, as well as research in which he expressed views that were inconsistent with privately expressed negative views", including reports on GoTo.com "materially misleading because they were contrary to privately expressed negative views". Grubman "issued fraudulent, misleading, and otherwise flawed research reports under SSB's name", with "recommendations contrary to the actual views regarding the companies" and growth predicted "without a reasonable basis".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was underwriting business won on the strength of coverage, and the settlement prices it: ten firms paying "$875 million in penalties and disgorgement", plus "$432.5 million to fund independent research" and "$80 million from seven of the firms" for investor education — "The total of all payments is roughly $1.4 billion."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment has two features worth naming because they cut against the usual pattern. The firms "will not seek reimbursement or indemnification for any penalties that they pay" and "will not seek a tax deduction or tax credit ... for any penalty amounts" — closing the two routes by which a penalty is normally passed on. Against that: the allegations were neither admitted nor denied, and the two individuals named settled rather than being tried.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: An integrated investment bank in which research is a cost centre justified by the banking revenue it helps win, and published ratings are the firm’s product rather than the analyst’s opinion.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The structural separation imposed by the settlement — "separating the research and investment banking departments at the firms", changing how research is reviewed and supervised, and "making independent research available to investors", funded by $432.5 million from the firms themselves.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Favourable coverage won mandates; mandates paid for the research department; the research department produced the coverage. The investor reading the rating was the only party to the loop who was not inside it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the dot-com crash was mass delusion — everybody believed, everybody was wrong, and nobody did anything improper — or, inverted, that it was a single orchestrated pump in which every analyst was bought.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The delusion reading fails on the regulators’ central charge, which is not error but divergence: research "inconsistent with privately expressed negative views", reports "contrary to privately expressed negative views", "recommendations contrary to the actual views regarding the companies". People who are merely wrong do not hold a different view privately. The orchestration reading fails on the shape of the actions: they allege inappropriate influence of banking over research and supervisory deficiencies at the firms, not a coordinated scheme among them, and the specific fraud findings attach to named individuals at two firms. Note too that the allegations against the firms were neither admitted nor denied, and both individuals settled; none of this was tried.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A global settlement completed on 28 April 2003 by the SEC, the New York Attorney General, NASAA, NASD, the NYSE and state regulators against ten named firms — Bear Stearns, CSFB, Goldman Sachs, Lehman Brothers, J.P. Morgan Securities, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup Global Markets, UBS Warburg and U.S. Bancorp Piper Jaffray. $875 million in penalties and disgorgement, $432.5 million for independent research, $80 million for investor education, roughly $1.4 billion in all; no indemnification and no tax deduction for penalties. Findings of inappropriate influence by investment banking over research from approximately mid-1999 through mid-2001 or later, and supervisory deficiencies at every firm. Henry Blodget censured, permanently barred and paying $4 million; Jack Grubman censured, permanently barred and paying $15 million, both for research contrary to their privately held views. And the structural remedy: separation of research from investment banking, with independent research made available to investors.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "Ten of Nation’s Top Investment Firms Settle Enforcement Actions Involving Conflicts of Interest Between Research and Investment Banking", Release 2003-54, 28 April 2003
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. The announcement, made jointly by the SEC chairman, the New York Attorney General, NASAA, NASD, the NYSE and state regulators, completed "the global settlement in principle reached and announced by regulators last December", following "joint investigations by the regulators of allegations of undue influence of investment banking interests on securities research at brokerage firms." THE TEN FIRMS ARE NAMED: Bear Stearns, Credit Suisse First Boston, Goldman Sachs, Lehman Brothers, J.P. Morgan Securities, Merrill Lynch, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup Global Markets (formerly Salomon Smith Barney), UBS Warburg and U.S. Bancorp Piper Jaffray. THE MONEY: "the ten firms will pay a total of $875 million in penalties and disgorgement, consisting of $387.5 million in disgorgement and $487.5 million in penalties (which includes Merrill Lynch's previous payment of $100 million ...)". Half of the $775 million paid by the firms other than Merrill Lynch goes "into a fund to benefit customers of the firms" and the remainder to the states; the firms also pay "$432.5 million to fund independent research" and "$80 million from seven of the firms will fund and promote investor education", with "The total of all payments ... roughly $1.4 billion." TWO TERMS WORTH KEEPING: "the firms will not seek reimbursement or indemnification for any penalties that they pay", and "the firms will not seek a tax deduction or tax credit ... for any penalty amounts that they pay under the settlement." THE FINDING: "The enforcement actions allege that, from approximately mid-1999 through mid-2001 or later, all of the firms engaged in acts and practices that created or maintained inappropriate influence by investment banking over research analysts, thereby imposing conflicts of interest on research analysts that the firms failed to manage in an adequate or appropriate manner. In addition, the regulators found supervisory deficiencies at every firm." The structural remedy included "separating the research and investment banking departments at the firms" and "making independent research available to investors". The release states the allegations were neither admitted nor denied. citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, NASD and NYSE, "Permanently Bar Henry Blodget From the Securities Industry and Require $4 Million Payment", Release 2003-56, 28 April 2003
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. Henry Blodget, "a former managing director at Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Incorporated and the senior research analyst and group head for the Internet sector at the firm, will be censured and permanently barred from the securities industry, and will make a total payment of $4 million to settle the charges against him." THE CHARGE: "The regulators charged that, among other things, Blodget, of New York City, issued fraudulent research under Merrill Lynch's name, as well as research in which he expressed views that were inconsistent with privately expressed negative views." The standard he is said to have breached is set out: published research reports must "have a reasonable basis, present a fair picture of the investment risks and benefits, and not make exaggerated or unwarranted claims." Specifically, during 1999-2001 he "aided and abetted violations of antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws and violated SRO rules by issuing research reports on one internet company (GoTo.com) that were materially misleading because they were contrary to privately expressed negative views", and issued reports on six further internet companies including InfoSpace, 24/7 Media and Lifeminders. A settlement of charges, not an adjudicated verdict. citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, New York Attorney General’s Office, NASD and NYSE, "Permanently Bar Jack Grubman and Require $15 Million Payment", Release 2003-55, 28 April 2003
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. Jack Grubman "will be censured and permanently barred from the securities industry, and will pay a total of $15 million to settle their charges against him." The regulators charged that Grubman, "a former managing director of Salomon Smith Barney Inc. (SSB), the lead research analyst for SSB's telecommunications (telecom) sector and the linchpin for SSB's investment banking efforts in the telecom sector, issued fraudulent, misleading, and otherwise flawed research reports under SSB's name. As a result, Grubman aided and abetted SSB's violations of antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws and violated NASD and NYSE rules as well as New York State law." The phrase "the linchpin for SSB's investment banking efforts in the telecom sector" is the regulators’, and it is the conflict stated as a job description. Specifically, during 1999-2001 he "issued several fraudulent research reports on two telecom stocks (Focal Communications and Metromedia Fiber) that contained misstatements and omissions of material facts about the companies, contained recommendations contrary to the actual views regarding the companies, overlooked or minimized the risk of investing in these companies, and predicted substantial growth in the companies' revenues and earnings without a reasonable basis", and issued reports on six telecom stocks including RCN, Level 3, XO, Adelphia Business Solutions and Williams Communications "that were not based on principles of fair dealing and good faith". A settlement of charges, not an adjudicated verdict.
